foresee

/for-SEE/ — stress on second syllable, rhymes with free · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To foresee something is to know or realize that it is going to happen before it actually occurs.

Nobody could foresee that the tiny startup would become a global company.

Example

The climate scientist studied rising temperatures and atmospheric changes, and could foresee that coastal cities would face serious flooding within decades.

Foresee is more precise than predict or expect—it carries the sense of knowing something will happen based on evidence, not just guessing or hoping. The scientist doesn't hope; she knows what's coming based on data.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

anticipate: To anticipate something is to act before it arrives — stocking up ahead of a shortage, rescheduling ahead of a strike. To foresee it is only to know early that it is coming: foreseeing lives in the mind, while anticipating shows up in what you do.

forecast: To forecast is to announce in advance what the data suggest will happen — forecasts are published for others to plan around. To foresee is quieter and more personal: one mind realizing early what is coming, whether or not a word of it is ever shared.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

overlook: fail to notice or consider something

disregard: pay no attention to warning signs

Where it sits · how clearly the future is known

wonder → expect → predict → foresee

wonder vs. foresee: Wonder is far weaker than foresee: wondering means merely asking yourself what might happen, while foreseeing means realizing it will happen before it does.

expect vs. foresee: Expect is weaker than foresee: expecting means thinking something will probably occur, while foreseeing means clearly realizing it is coming before the signs are obvious to anyone else.

predict vs. foresee: Predict sits just below foresee: predicting means committing to a claim about what will happen, while foreseeing means genuinely knowing it is coming before it occurs.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — fore-: before, ahead of time (Old English)

Root — see: to perceive with the eyes (from seon) (Old English)

Put it together: Foresee is exactly what it looks like: fore- ('before') plus see. To foresee something is to 'see it beforehand' — to know or realize it is going to happen before it actually occurs.

Use the root in a new word: foresight: Packing a flashlight before the storm hit turned out to be real foresight on Dad's part.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Foresee is stronger and more certain than predict or expect. Use it when someone knows (not just guesses) what will happen, usually because they've read the signs or have relevant expertise. For uncertain guesses or planning, 'predict' or 'anticipate' are often better choices.
